item.title: Replay Is a Family of Assertions: Fork-Safety in Event-Sourced Agent Runtimes
item.description: arXiv:2611.06924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Event-sourced agent runtimes commonly claim deterministic replay, cheap forking, and lineage. These are families of assertions, not one guarantee. A fixed-log fold may be deterministic while reactive settlement remains schedule-sensitive; a recorded oracle result can enable zero-call replay while the original interaction still changed cost or world state; and a prefix copy cannot undo an action in a discarded suffix. We present an executable F# contract that separates facts from effect requests, makes scheduling explicit, and assesses a cut relative to projection, strict execution replay, external continuation, or a declared counterfactual-world observation. Preserved counterexamples show that general settlement is neither terminating nor confluent and that disjoint declared writes do not prevent read/trigger interference. Against 5,540 public runtime logs, all 317,296 projection cuts satisfy the stated observation, while 36,251 cuts split a model request and do not license continuation; another 120,969 are Conditional because a committed oracle result must be served from the record without re-execution. In 121 observed forks, 16,625 retained-prefix events have zero structural mismatches, but none crosses an external-effect boundary. A separate public offline conformance fork crosses a committed, recorded oracle boundary. Its generator observes that the inherited result is served without a second fixture-oracle call; its verifier checks receipt/log consistency and a fork-bound HMAC assertion under a public conformance key. The result reframes cheap forking as a property-indexed semantic contract with explicit evidence and environment preconditions.
item.dc:creator: Yohei Nakajima

item.title: SymFC: Configurable Semantics for All Paths Symbolic Execution in Haskell via Embeddings
item.description: arXiv:2611.07916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lightweight methods like QuickCheck have proven to be successful in functional languages and beyond, as they let users specify properties as Boolean functions directly in code. We can replicate some of their benefits for (bounded) proofs via symbolic execution. If we can execute arbitrary functions symbolically, we can specify properties just as easily. Unfortunately, existing symbolic execution tools for Haskell are restricted to a subset of the language that excludes many real-world applications like IO; they also have a hard time scaling to larger programs, making them a poor fit for general purpose lightweight verification. One reason behind these limitations is that existing techniques only offer fixed symbolic semantics for SMT base types. This makes it hard to cover more programming constructs and libraries; it also makes it difficult to fine-tune symbolic representations for better performance. We present SymFC, a new symbolic execution method for Haskell that offers configurable semantics via embeddings. An embedding of a function in SymFC is just another Haskell function that can use arbitrary code, as well as SMT primitives. Embeddings make it easy to support new programming constructs and fine-tune symbolic representations for speed. To integrate embeddings into Haskell's type system, we make use of Haskell's coercions, which let us transparently convert between a Haskell type and the type of its embedding. We realize embeddings in SymFC, an all-paths symbolic execution engine for Haskell, which lets us symbolically represent arbitrary types and values in GHC core. We implement SymFC as a GHC plugin, and evaluate it by checking properties of Haskell's container library, and the iproute library. We build embeddings for IORef, Haskell's Ptr/ForeignPtr interface, and the hardware library Clash, and our evaluation reports a 6.25x speedup on G2's own benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Robin Webbers, Wind Wong, Klaus v. Gleissenthall

item.title: GUARDTs: Decentralized Access Control for Replicated Data Types
item.description: arXiv:2611.08083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Replicated data types providing strong eventual consistency offer a principled foundation for developing decentralized software. Yet existing approaches to programming such data types leave access control unresolved: they either provide none at all, delegate it to a trusted coordinator, reintroducing the centralization they were designed to avoid, or tie it to specific data-type constructions, while typically assuming non-Byzantine replicas and static policies. We present GUARDTs: Guarded Unforgeable Algebraic Replicated Data Types, which embed fine-grained permissions directly into the application data model, operate without a central authority, support dynamic policy evolution, and tolerate Byzantine replicas. We formally prove that GUARDTs guarantee confidentiality, integrity, and availability and show empirically that their access control adds negligible overhead on top of the cost of Byzantine-resilient replication itself.
item.dc:creator: Christian Kuessner, Ragnar Mogk, Julian Haas, Annette Bieniusa, Mira Mezini

item.title: NUMA-Torch: Compiler-Driven NUMA-Aware LLM Prefill on Multi-Socket CPUs
item.description: arXiv:2611.07105v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For sufficiently large transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs), whose parameters cannot be retained in on-chip caches, prefill throughput on multi-socket CPUs is often limited by sustainable DRAM bandwidth rather than peak floating-point throughput. In the standard PyTorch compilation (i.e., TorchInductor) path, model weights are allocated without considering the Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) topology: specifically, the affinity between memory banks and compute cores is disregarded. This causes a substantial fraction of weight accesses to traverse the inter-socket interconnect, severely degrading the effective memory bandwidth available to each socket. We address this bottleneck through a compiler-level solution that makes TorchInductor NUMA-aware. Treating each NUMA socket as an independent tensor-parallel partition, we introduce NUMA-aware Tensor Parallelism (NUMA-TP). This approach transparently shards weights across sockets and schedules compute kernels such that thread pools and memory allocations remain strictly local to their respective sockets using CPU affinity. We evaluate the approach on GPT-2 (117M, 345M, 762M) and BERT (Small, Large), which exercise standard multi-head attention and MLP, as well as Gemma 3 270M, which combines Multi-Query Attention with a GeGLU-gated MLP. By strictly enforcing data locality, our approach successfully mitigates cross-socket traffic, achieving prefill speedups of up to 2.63x on a dual-socket Haswell platform, up to 1.87x on a dual-socket Cascade Lake platform, and up to 2.27x on a four-socket Haswell-EX platform.
item.dc:creator: Thisara Rathnayaka Weerakoon (Department of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka), Ishan Dewpura (Department of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka), Niman Ransindu (Department of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka), Shavin Anjitha (Department of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka), Tharindu R. Patabandi (Independent Researcher, San Jose, CA, USA), Sanath Jayasena (Department of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka)

item.title: TauLang: A Language and Compiler for Space-Time Programming on Statically Scheduled Accelerators
item.description: arXiv:2611.06079v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Statically scheduled accelerators such as Groq's Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) achieve low-latency large language model inference by stripping dynamic synchronization hardware from the chip. With no caches, arbiters, or hardware schedulers, the compiler must fix the exact slice and issue cycle of every operation, so when an operation runs is a condition for correctness. Existing kernel languages cannot target such machines because they rely on hardware to resolve cycle timing and instead encode schedules implicitly in code structure. We present TauLang, a kernel language and compiler that makes time a first-class citizen of the program. The programmer schedules operations, loops, and composed kernels with parameterized explicit times, so exploring schedules means changing parameter values rather than rewriting code. TauLang validates explicit times algebraically in TauIR, its timed intermediate representation. It then solves tensor placement and cycle scheduling jointly in an integer linear program, using explicit times to group connected operations into timing clusters that prune the search space. On a cycleaccurate model of a TSP-like machine, joint search achieves a $1.40\times$ latency speedup across ten kernels over a space-first flow. A few explicit time pins keep latency within one cycle of the untimed schedules and scale joint search to 1,636 GEMM blocks, whereas untimed search finds no schedule at 32.
item.dc:creator: Xuxiao Yang, Junchi Wu, Yuqi Peng, Feiyang Wu, Zhuoran Li, Wei Kong, Shuo Tao, Dongyi Fan, Yiming Zhang, Keqin Luo, Xingrui Gao, Xuehai Qian, Youwei Zhuo
